title: Hatching Eggs
strapline: Real eggs in an incubator, checked every morning — the longest and best wait of the year.
intent: Children learn about animal life cycles and change by watching one happen in front of them.
A twenty-one day wait builds patience and anticipation nothing else in the year matches.
Daily checking and recording builds the habit of careful, repeated observation.
Children learn to handle fragile living things with real gentleness and care.
The arrival of a chick provokes genuine questions about life, growth and care.
implementation: Set up real eggs in an incubator where children can see but not reach the controls.
Agree with the children how the eggs will be checked and recorded each day.
Track changes each day on a shared chart — day number, what we noticed.
Explain the process honestly, including that not every egg will hatch.
Teach and enforce gentle handling before any chick arrives, not after.
Guide children to notice small changes rather than expecting drama daily.
Arrange the aftercare properly and tell children where the chicks will go and why.
key_questions: What do you think is happening inside the egg today?
How many days have we been waiting? How many more?
How should we hold a chick to keep it safe?
What does the chick need now it has hatched?
What else do you know that starts as an egg?

impact.text: Children observe a life cycle and can tell you about it.
Children treat living things gently as a matter of course.
Children build curiosity, patience and careful observation over weeks.
Children count and compare days, tracking a number that matters to them.
Children ask real questions about living things and expect real answers.
Children show care and kindness towards a vulnerable creature.

enhancements: A day-by-day photo diary displayed at child height and added to each morning.
A life-cycle sequencing set — egg, chick, hen — to order and re-order.
A comparison with the frogspawn or caterpillar life cycle running alongside.
A candling session, if the equipment allows, to see inside the egg safely.
A book basket of life-cycle non-fiction beside the incubator.
A "what does a chick need?" list the children write and check off.

playing_exploring: Children investigate the incubator and the eggs with intense curiosity.
Every day brings something genuinely new to notice.
active_learning: Children sustain interest across three weeks of very slow change.
They take the daily checking seriously as their own job.
creating_thinking: Children predict when the eggs will hatch and what will emerge.
They connect the egg to other life cycles they have met.
